lead: A property is any quantity that has a definite value when the system is in a given condition, such as pressure, temperature or specific volume. The set of property values at one instant is the state. A change from one state to another is a process, the series of states passed through is its path, and a series of processes that brings the system back to its first state is a cycle. The state postulate says how many properties you must know to fix a state, an equation of state links them, and a state diagram turns every state into a point and every slow process into a line. Heat and work, unlike properties, depend on the path.
prereq: You need: systems and boundaries. Equilibrium, which a state needs, is the next chapter.

blocks.text: Split a system in equilibrium into two equal halves. A property that keeps its value in each half is intensive: pressure p, temperature T, density ρ. A property that halves is extensive: mass m, volume V, internal energy U, enthalpy H. An extensive property divided by mass is a specific property, written in lower case, and behaves like an intensive one.

blocks.where: v is specific volume in m³/kg; V is volume in m³; m is mass in kg; ρ is density in kg/m³. In the same way u = U/m and h = H/m in kJ/kg.

blocks.text: A property depends only on the state, never on how the system got there. That gives a test: a quantity is a property if, and only if, its change between two states is the same for every path. Its change around any cycle is zero: ∮dX = 0.

sections.h3: The state postulate and the equation of state

blocks.text: How many properties fix a state? For a simple compressible system, one in which the only important way of doing work is volume change (no electric, magnetic, surface-tension or motion effects), the state postulate answers: two independent intensive properties fix the state. Once you know p and v, or p and T, or T and v, every other property has one value, which you read from a table or a chart or calculate.

Two properties are independent when one can change while the other is held constant. In a single phase, p and T are independent. During boiling they are not: water at 101.325 kPa boils at about 100 °C whatever its dryness, so p and T together do not fix how much is liquid and how much vapour. A second property such as specific volume or dryness fraction is needed; pure substances and steam tables develop this.
An equation of state is a formula that links p, v and T. The simplest is the ideal gas equation, good for air and most gases at low pressure and high temperature:
pv = RT,   pV = mRT,   R = R̄ / M
blocks.where: p is absolute pressure in kPa; v is specific volume in m³/kg; T is absolute temperature in K; R is the gas constant in kJ/(kg·K); R̄ = 8.314 kJ/(kmol·K) is the universal gas constant; M is the molar mass in kg/kmol. For air M ≈ 28.97, so R = 8.314 ÷ 28.97 = 0.287 kJ/(kg·K).

blocks.text: Given any two of p, v and T, the equation gives the third: the state postulate at work.

sections.h3: State diagrams: states as points, processes as lines

blocks.text: Because two properties fix the state, a state can be drawn as a point on a graph of any two properties: a state diagram. The common ones are the p–v (or p–V) diagram, the T–v diagram and the p–T diagram; the T–s and h–s diagrams follow once entropy is defined. A state drawn this way is a state point.
A process made of equilibrium states, a quasi-static process, appears as a continuous line between two state points. Processes are named by the property held constant, and each has a typical line:

items: isochoric (constant volume): a vertical line on p–V;
isobaric (constant pressure): a horizontal line on p–V;
isothermal (constant temperature): for an ideal gas the curve pV = constant on p–V;
adiabatic (no heat transfer): a steeper curve on p–V for a slow ideal-gas process.

blocks.text: A cycle is a closed loop.

Point functions (properties) change by the same amount on every path between two states. Path functions, heat Q and work W, do not: they are energy crossing the boundary during a process, and their amount depends on the route. Their small amounts are written δQ and δW, not dQ and dW, to show they are inexact differentials. On a p–V diagram the work of a slow process is the area under its line, so two different lines between the same states give different work (Figure 1.3.1).

After one full cycle every property is back to its first value, so ΔT = 0, Δp = 0, ΔV = 0 and ΔU = 0 over the cycle. The net work need not be zero: it equals the area enclosed by the loop, positive when the loop is traced clockwise on a p–V diagram. That non-zero net work is what every engine is built to deliver.

figure.caption: The worked example’s cycle for 0.2323 kg of air: four states, each a point fixed by p and V, with its temperature from pV = mRT. The two routes from state 1 to state 3 give the same temperature rise but different work, and the loop encloses a net work of 10 kJ.

spec.aria: A pressure–volume diagram with a rectangle: state 1 at 0.20 cubic metres and 100 kPa (300 K), state 2 at 0.20 and 200 kPa (600 K), state 3 at 0.30 and 200 kPa (900 K), state 4 at 0.30 and 100 kPa (450 K). The enclosed area, 10 kJ, is shaded.

examples.question: Air (R = 0.287 kJ/(kg·K)) in a cylinder is taken round the cycle 1→2→3→4→1: state 1 is 100 kPa, 0.20 m³, 300 K; heating at constant volume to 200 kPa (state 2); expansion at constant pressure to 0.30 m³ (state 3); cooling at constant volume to 100 kPa (state 4); compression at constant pressure back to state 1. (a) Find the mass of air and its specific volume at state 1. (b) Find the temperature at states 2, 3 and 4. (c) Show that the net change of temperature over the cycle is zero. (d) Compare the work done along 1→2→3 and along 1→4→3, and find the net work of the cycle.
steps: Each state was fixed by two properties, p and V for the known mass, and the equation of state gave the third: the state postulate in use.
(c) Temperature changes: 1→2 +300 K, 2→3 +300 K, 3→4 −450 K, 4→1 −150 K. Sum: 300 + 300 − 450 − 150 = 0 K. Temperature is a property, so its net change round a cycle is zero.
(d) Work on each line, from the area under it (W = p ΔV for constant pressure, zero for constant volume): W₁₂ = 0; W₂₃ = 200 × (0.30 − 0.20) = 20 kJ; W₃₄ = 0; W₄₁ = 100 × (0.20 − 0.30) = −10 kJ.

Path 1→2→3: W = 0 + 20 = 20 kJ. Path 1→4→3: W = W₁₄ + W₄₃ = 100 × (0.30 − 0.20) + 0 = 10 kJ. The same two end states, the same ΔT = 900 − 300 = 600 K on both paths, but different work: work is a path function.
Net work of the cycle: 0 + 20 + 0 − 10 = 10 kJ, the area of the rectangle, 100 kPa × 0.10 m³. The loop runs clockwise on the p–V diagram, so the net work is done by the air.
examples.answer: m = 0.2323 kg and v₁ = 0.861 m³/kg; T₂ = 600 K, T₃ = 900 K, T₄ = 450 K; ∮dT = 0; W = 20 kJ on 1→2→3 and 10 kJ on 1→4→3; net cycle work 10 kJ.

traps: Heat and work are not properties. A sentence such as 'the heat in the gas' is wrong; the gas has internal energy, and heat is energy crossing the boundary.
Two properties fix the state only if they are independent. During a phase change p and T are tied together, so use p and dryness fraction (or v) instead.
Specific volume v is in m³/kg and volume V is in m³; pv = RT uses v, pV = mRT uses V. Mixing them gives answers off by the mass.
Zero net change of every property over a cycle does not mean zero net work or heat: the cycle in Figure 1.3.1 delivers 10 kJ.

quiz.q: Define intensive and extensive properties with one example each.
quiz.a: Intensive: independent of the amount of matter, such as pressure or temperature. Extensive: proportional to the amount, such as volume or mass.

quiz.q: State the state postulate for a simple compressible system.
quiz.a: The state of a simple compressible system is fixed by two independent intensive properties.

quiz.q: Why is heat called a path function?
quiz.a: Heat is energy crossing the boundary during a process; its amount depends on the route between the end states, not on the states alone, so it has no value at a state.

quiz.q: Find the specific volume of air at 200 kPa and 450 K (R = 0.287 kJ/(kg·K)).
In the worked example, the air goes from state 1 to state 3 by two routes. Compare ΔU and W on the two routes.
quiz.a: ΔU is the same on both because U is a property and the end states are the same. W is 20 kJ on 1→2→3 and 10 kJ on 1→4→3, because work is the area under the path and the paths differ.

quiz.q: A quantity X changes by +5 units along one path from A to B and by +8 units along another. Can X be a property? Explain.
quiz.a: No. A property changes by the same amount on every path between two states, so its round trip A→B→A by different paths would give a net change of 5 − 8 = −3 units, not zero.

beyond: Property software, such as the IAPWS formulations for water and steam, uses many-term equations of state to give v, u, h and s from any two independent properties. Systems with extra work modes, magnetic or electrical, need more independent properties. Search next: state postulate, equations of state, IAPWS-IF97.
